formation.title: The Cities of the Coast
formation.text:
The banner of Dalmatia flies over the ancient cities of the eastern Adriatic. From Zadar in the north to Dubrovnik in the south, a chain of fortified port cities clings to the narrow coastal strip between the Dinaric Mountains and the sea. For centuries these communes have balanced between empires (Byzantium, Venice, Hungary, and now the Ottoman shadow), surviving through commerce, seamanship, and an instinct for diplomacy that borders on art.

Dubrovnik's Great Council must now decide the character of this new union. Shall Dalmatia follow the Ragusan model: a republic of merchants and diplomats, paying tribute to preserve autonomy, thriving on trade that flows between East and West? Or shall the coastal cities unite their fleets into a maritime league, building naval power that commands the Adriatic through force of arms rather than force of argument?

This choice unlocks a destiny path in the Traditions tab.

options.text: Liberty is not given; it is traded for

modifiers.name: Republic of the Adriatic
modifiers.text: Following the model of Ragusa, Dalmatia governs itself as a mercantile republic, preserving its freedom through shrewd diplomacy, trade agreements, and the careful balancing of greater powers, paying tribute where necessary, but bowing to none.

options.text: The sea shall be our shield and sword

modifiers.name: Dalmatian Maritime League
modifiers.text: The city-states of the Dalmatian coast unite into a naval confederation, pooling their shipyards, sailors, and merchant fleets into a force that commands the Adriatic sea lanes and projects power far beyond their modest coastline.

advances.name: Fondaco Tradition
advances.text: The fondaco, a combined warehouse, exchange, and hostelry, is the foundation of Dalmatian commerce, where merchants store goods, negotiate contracts, and settle disputes under the watchful eye of the commune.

advances.name: Book of All Reformations
advances.text: From 1335 every amendment the councils make to the old statute is entered in a single book, the Liber Omnium Reformationum. A merchant, native or foreign, can learn the law as it stands today and not as it stood in his grandfather's time.

advances.name: Closing of the Great Council
advances.text: Since 1332 the Great Council of Ragusa is closed. Only men of the noble houses sit in it, each from his eighteenth year, and every office of the commune is filled from among them, for a short term.

advances.name: Salt Monopoly
advances.text: The saltworks of Pag, Ston, and Nin produce the white gold of the Adriatic, a commodity so valuable that control of the salt trade underpins Dalmatian wealth and diplomacy.

advances.name: Uskok Tradition
advances.text: The Uskoks, refugees from Ottoman-conquered lands, settle along the Dalmatian coast as frontier fighters, their guerrilla skills and knowledge of mountain terrain making them invaluable border defenders.

advances.name: Hospital of Mercy
advances.text: In 1432 the Republic opens a foundling hospital, among the first in Europe: a child left at its door is nursed and raised at the commune's cost. It joins the almshouse of 1347 and the physicians the commune has kept on salary since 1301.

event.title: The Health Officers
event.text:
The commune keeps physicians on salary, an almshouse and now a hospital for foundlings. It also keeps, since 1390, officers of health chosen from the patricians, whom the people call the cazamorti. Plague is reported again in the hinterland, and the officers ask the council for a free hand: to turn back caravans at the gates, to hold every ship and its crew apart for the full term, to burn suspect bales and to flog or fine whoever slips past them.

The merchants answer that the city lives by its trade. A port that holds every cargo for weeks will see the ships go elsewhere. They would have the physicians inspect arrivals and let the healthy pass. Shall the health officers rule the gates and the harbour, accepting slower commerce for safer citizens? Or shall the port stay open, trusting the physicians to manage the risk while trade flows?

options.text: The health officers shall have their free hand

modifiers.name: Rule of the Health Officers
modifiers.text: The officers of health hold the gates and the harbour: caravans are turned back, crews are held apart for the full term and suspect goods are burned. The population is protected at the cost of slower trade.

options.text: Commerce must not be chained at the gate

modifiers.name: Open Port Policy
modifiers.text: The port stays open and the commune's physicians inspect arrivals in place of holding them apart. Trade prospers, though disease finds easier entry.

advances.name: Ragusan Diplomacy
advances.text: The Republic of Ragusa perfected the art of survival through diplomacy, maintaining agents and informants across the Mediterranean while playing Venice, Hungary, and the Ottomans against each other.

advances.name: Abolition Decree
advances.text: In 1416, the Republic of Ragusa became the first European state to abolish the slave trade, a declaration of principle that enhanced its prestige and attracted skilled freemen to its harbors.

event.title: The Abolition Decree
event.text:
On 27 January 1416, the Great Council of Ragusa passed a decree that would not be matched by any European state for nearly four centuries. The slave trade is hereby abolished within the Republic. No Ragusan ship may transport slaves. No Ragusan citizen may buy, sell, or own another human being. The penalty is six months imprisonment and a fine of twenty-five pounds per person.

The motivations are mixed: genuine moral conviction among some councilors, practical calculation among others who note that slave labor depresses wages for free workers, and diplomatic advantage in presenting Ragusa as a beacon of civilization. Whatever the reasons, the result is the same: Ragusa becomes the first European state to ban the slave trade, a full 391 years before Britain.

options.text: Non bene pro toto libertas venditur auro

modifiers.name: Liberty of Ragusa
modifiers.text: The abolition decree of 1416, 'Non bene pro toto libertas venditur auro' (Liberty is not sold for all the gold in the world), earns Ragusa international prestige and attracts skilled workers from across the Mediterranean.

advances.name: Adriatic Salt Routes
advances.text: Dalmatian salt from Pag, Ston, and Nin travels the Adriatic trade routes, exchanged for Italian grain, Levantine spices, and Balkan minerals. The pans are the commune's own: those of Ston alone are worth 15,900 ducats a year to Ragusa.

advances.name: Twenty-Four Carats
advances.text: Every Ragusan ship is owned in twenty-four carats, shares held by patricians, captains, widows and convents alike, so that half the city has money at sea. The great carracks the English call argosies are laid down on that money: armed merchantmen that need no escort.

event.title: The Argosy Fleet
event.text:
The word 'argosy' has entered the languages of Europe as a synonym for a great merchant fleet, and it derives from 'Ragusa.' The reason is plain to see in the harbor of Dubrovnik. One hundred and eighty ships, crewed by five thousand sailors, carry Dalmatian goods to every port in the Mediterranean and beyond. The largest argosies are four-masted vessels carrying one hundred tons, armed with cannon and crewed by one hundred forty men.

Shakespeare himself will immortalize these ships. Spanish admirals recruit Ragusan captains for their armadas. The argosies are not merely merchant vessels: they are floating fortresses that need no naval escort, combining the cargo capacity of a merchantman with the armament of a warship.

Shall we organize these ships into a merchant armada, projecting power through their sheer size and armament? Or shall we perfect the convoy system, emphasizing trade protection and efficient commerce over raw naval might?

options.text: Each argosy is a castle on the waves

modifiers.name: Merchant Armada
modifiers.text: The Ragusan argosies are organized as a merchant armada: armed merchantmen so heavily built that they need no escort, projecting both commercial and military power across the Mediterranean.

options.text: Our strength is in the convoy, not the broadside

modifiers.name: Convoy System
modifiers.text: Ragusan merchant ships sail in organized convoys, with light escorts and standardized sailing schedules that maximize trade throughput while minimizing losses to pirates and privateers.

advances.name: Statute of Poljica
advances.text: In the hills behind Split the twelve villages of Poljica keep a statute of their own, written down in 1440, and choose their own grand count. Their men hold the passes above the coast: Ottoman armies are turned back there in 1530 and again in 1686.

advances.name: Sponza Archives
advances.text: The Sponza Palace in Dubrovnik houses the state archive and customs office, where meticulous records of trade, diplomacy, and governance preserve centuries of Ragusan knowledge and enable efficient customs collection.

advances.name: Tribute Autonomy
advances.text: Dalmatia pays tribute to the Ottoman Empire (12,500 gold ducats annually) in exchange for internal autonomy and trading privileges across Ottoman lands, a pragmatic bargain that preserves freedom at a price.

advances.name: Bracera Fleet
advances.text: The bracera, a swift, shallow-draft galley with eight oars and a crew of thirty, can cover a hundred sea miles in a night, outmaneuvering the heavy Venetian galleys in the narrow bays and inlets of the Adriatic coast.

advances.name: Scala of Split
advances.text: In 1592 the scala of Split is opened on the plan of the merchant Daniel Rodriga: a customs house, warehouses and lodgings at the head of the road from Bosnia. The caravans of the Balkan interior come down to the quay and their goods are shipped across the Adriatic, so that a harbour of fishermen becomes one of the busiest on the coast.

advances.name: Pharmacy Tradition
advances.text: The Franciscan pharmacy of Dubrovnik, operating continuously since 1317, is among the oldest in Europe, pioneering the preparation of remedies from Adriatic herbs and Mediterranean plants.

advances.name: Silk and Dye Trade
advances.text: The fondaci deal in the silk and dyes of the Levant. Outside the Pile gate, where Pietro Pantella of Piacenza first set up his looms, the dye house and the weavers turn wool into fine cloth for re-export.

advances.name: Fleet Zenith
advances.text: At its peak, the Ragusan merchant fleet numbers 180 ships crewed by 5,000 sailors. When the great carracks grow too costly to keep, the owners turn to the pulaka: a roomy three-masted trader that a small crew can sail to the Levant and back.

advances.name: General School of Zadar
advances.text: The Dominicans of Zadar have kept a general school since 1396: the first place of higher learning on the eastern shore of the Adriatic. The sons of the coast read philosophy and theology there before they sail for Padua.

advances.name: Walled Cities
advances.text: The massive walls of Dubrovnik, Split, and Zadar (some dating to Roman times, continuously maintained and expanded) make the Dalmatian cities virtually impregnable to siege.

advances.name: Mercantile Banking
advances.text: Ragusan banking houses extend credit to merchants across the Adriatic, financing trade ventures in the Balkan interior and the Levant with bills that are honoured from Ancona to Alexandria.

advances.name: Kraglski Dalmatin
advances.text: In 1806 the first newspaper in the Croatian language is printed at Zadar, in two columns, Italian and Croatian. For the first time the coast reads the news of the world in the tongue it speaks at home.

advances.name: Citizen Brotherhoods
advances.text: The merchants who are not noble are enrolled in two brotherhoods, the Antunini and the Lazarini. Shut out of the councils, they hold a great part of the carats in the fleet that sails under Saint Blaise in the eighteenth century, and a voyage is financed in their halls.

advances.name: Port Modernization
advances.text: New moles, expanded quays and bonded warehouses fit the ancient harbors of the Dalmatian coast for a new age of shipping, and in 1818 the first light of the coast is lit on the cape at Savudrija.

advances.name: Constitutional Reform
advances.text: The ancient republican traditions of the Dalmatian communes are formalized into modern constitutional governance, with codified rights, representative assemblies, and professional bureaucracy.

destiny.name: Dalmatian Destiny
destiny.text: The cities of the Dalmatian coast have united under a single banner. Whether through the arts of diplomacy or the strength of the fleet, this new state must now prove itself worthy of enduring among the great powers of the Mediterranean.

event.title: The Destiny of the Coast
event.text:
Dalmatia stands united: a chain of fortified port cities stretching from Istria to the Bay of Kotor, bound together by the sea that gives them life. The ancient motto of Ragusa, Non bene pro toto libertas venditur auro ('Liberty is not sold for all the gold in the world'), now serves as the watchword of an entire nation.

But liberty must be earned and defended, not merely proclaimed. The path ahead demands vision, resources, and the will to act. Whether Dalmatia shall endure as a republic of merchants or a league of warriors, only the choices of its rulers will determine.

destiny.name: Tribute and Trade
destiny.text: Secure the Adriatic approaches by bringing the ports of Kotor and Bar under Dalmatian influence, establishing the tribute-diplomacy model that preserved Ragusa's independence for centuries. A treasury of 1,000 gold will fund the necessary embassies and trade agreements.

conditions.text: Chose the Republic of the Adriatic destiny
Own Kotor, or a subject owns it
Own Bar, or a subject owns it

event.title: The Art of Tribute
event.text:
Dalmatia has secured the ports of the Gulf of Kotor, establishing the system of tributary diplomacy that Ragusa perfected over centuries. By paying measured tribute to greater powers while maintaining internal autonomy, the republic purchases what fortresses alone cannot guarantee: the freedom to trade, to govern, and to endure.

The consuls and ambassadors of Dalmatia are now established in every court that matters. They carry gifts calibrated to the penny, intelligence gathered from every harbor, and the quiet confidence of men who know that their small republic's survival depends on being more useful alive than conquered.

options.text: Tribute is the price of liberty

destiny.name: Mediterranean Emporium
destiny.text: Extend the Dalmatian commercial network to the Ionian Islands, securing Corfu as a gateway to the wider Mediterranean. Raise Corfu into a town and open a fondaco there, where our merchants store their goods and settle their bills, and accumulate 2,000 gold to underwrite the expansion of trade.

conditions.text: Own Kérkyra, or a subject owns it
We own Corfu and it has a Fondaco

event.title: The Mediterranean Emporium
event.text:
Dalmatian merchants now trade from the Adriatic to the Ionian Sea and beyond. With a fondaco open at Corfu and the island secured as a commercial staging post, Dalmatian argosies carry salt, cloth, and dyes to ports that once dealt only with Venice or Genoa.

The republic's growing wealth attracts both opportunity and scrutiny. Shall we invest in expanding our network of consulates and trade agents, building permanent diplomatic infrastructure across the Mediterranean? Or shall we perfect the art of tributary diplomacy, using our wealth to buy the autonomy and trading rights that keep the republic free?

modifiers.name: Consular Network
modifiers.text: A web of Dalmatian consulates and trade agents established across Mediterranean ports, providing diplomatic access and commercial intelligence that extends the republic's reach far beyond its modest borders.

modifiers.name: Tribute Mastery
modifiers.text: The perfected art of tributary diplomacy: using carefully measured payments and trade concessions to purchase autonomy from greater powers while quietly expanding Dalmatian commercial influence.

destiny.name: Libertas
destiny.text: Dalmatia aspires to the highest ideal of the Ragusan republic: Libertas, liberty that endures through wealth, wisdom, and the respect of nations. Establish commercial presence in Crete and on the Italian shore at Ancona, achieve international prestige of 75, and amass a treasury of 3,000 gold to prove the republic's permanence.

conditions.text: Own Candia, or a subject owns it
Own Ancona, or a subject owns it

event.title: Libertas Aeterna
event.text:
The dream of Ragusa has been fulfilled on a scale its founders could never have imagined. Dalmatia's commercial empire stretches from the Adriatic to the shores of Crete, its consulates line the ports of the Mediterranean, and its treasury overflows with the wealth of nations.

The republic's motto, Libertas, is no longer a prayer whispered behind city walls. It is a fact demonstrated by gold, by ships, and by the grudging respect of empires. But how shall this liberty be exercised? Shall Dalmatia become a beacon of civilization, its academies and law courts attracting the finest minds of Europe? Or shall the merchant princes consolidate their power, building an oligarchy of wealth that shapes the commerce of the Mediterranean?

modifiers.name: Beacon of Liberty
modifiers.text: Dalmatia as a shining example of republican civilization, its academies, law courts, and tolerance attracting the finest minds and most industrious people of the Mediterranean, though the republic's military preparedness suffers from its pacific orientation.

options.text: The merchants shall guide the republic

modifiers.name: Merchant Princes
modifiers.text: A powerful oligarchy of Dalmatian merchant families who control the republic's commercial empire, investing in infrastructure and financial instruments, though their focus on profit drives up the cost of maintaining standing armies.

destiny.name: Adriatic Dominion
destiny.text: The Maritime League must secure the eastern Adriatic coast by force. Conquer Durres and Shkoder to control the strait that separates the Adriatic from the wider Mediterranean, while building an army of at least 30,000 men to enforce Dalmatian claims.

conditions.text: Own Durrës, or a subject owns it
Own Shkodër, or a subject owns it

event.title: Masters of the Strait
event.text:
The Maritime League has seized control of the eastern Adriatic coast from Dalmatia to Albania. Durres and Shkoder now fly Dalmatian colors, giving the fleet control of the narrow strait that connects the Adriatic to the wider Mediterranean.

No ship enters or leaves the Adriatic without passing within range of Dalmatian galleys. Pirates who once preyed on coastal shipping find themselves hunted by bracera patrols that know every cove and inlet. The strait belongs to Dalmatia, and the commerce that flows through it pays toll to Dalmatian ports.

destiny.name: Thalassocracy
destiny.text: Project Dalmatian naval power deep into the eastern Mediterranean by seizing Thessaloniki, the great port of the Aegean. Maintain an army of 50,000 and a treasury of 2,000 gold to sustain this far-flung dominion.

conditions.text: Own Thessaloníki, or a subject owns it

event.title: Thalassocracy of the East
event.text:
Dalmatian naval power now extends deep into the Aegean. Thessaloniki, the great port that once served Byzantine and Ottoman emperors, answers to the Maritime League. The Dalmatian fleet, from its heavy argosies to its swift bracera galleys, patrols waters that Venice and Genoa once considered their private seas.

Shall we establish permanent naval patrols across the Adriatic and Aegean, hunting pirates and enforcing Dalmatian maritime law? Or shall we fortify our island holdings, building garrisons that ensure lasting control of strategic chokepoints?

modifiers.name: Adriatic Patrol
modifiers.text: Permanent Dalmatian naval patrols sweep the Adriatic and Aegean, hunting pirates, enforcing maritime law, and projecting the league's power across the eastern Mediterranean.

modifiers.name: Island Garrisons
modifiers.text: Fortified garrisons on strategic islands and coastal positions, ensuring Dalmatian control of key chokepoints and providing secure bases for the league's naval operations.

destiny.name: Mare Nostrum
destiny.text: The Maritime League aspires to nothing less than mastery of the Adriatic Sea. Conquer Venice itself, the ancient rival, and the great port of Bari on the Italian shore. Command an army of 75,000 men and achieve prestige of 75 to complete the transformation from coastal confederation to Mediterranean power.

conditions.text: Own Venice, or a subject owns it
Own Bari, or a subject owns it

event.title: Mare Nostrum
event.text:
Venice has fallen. The city of the doges, the ancient mistress of the Adriatic, now submits to the maritime league it once dismissed as a chain of fishing villages. With Bari on the Italian shore also under Dalmatian control, the entire Adriatic Sea is a Dalmatian lake.

The transformation is complete. From a confederation of coastal communes to the dominant naval power of the eastern Mediterranean, the Maritime League has achieved what centuries of Venetian diplomacy sought to prevent. How shall this new power project itself? As a seaborne empire ruled by the doge's authority, or as a professional military state commanded by fleet admirals?

modifiers.name: Doge of the Sea
modifiers.text: A seaborne empire ruled by the doge's naval authority, with the wealth of conquered ports funding the fleet and the plunder of rivals enriching the treasury.

modifiers.name: Fleet Admiral
modifiers.text: A professional military command structure with fleet admirals directing both naval and land operations, emphasizing rapid deployment, logistical efficiency, and sustained campaigning.

units.name: Uskok Raiders
units.text: Refugee guerrilla fighters from Ottoman-occupied Bosnia and Croatia. The Uskoks ('those who jumped in') specialize in mountain ambushes and coastal raids, using their intimate knowledge of the rugged terrain to devastating effect.

units.name: Men of Poljica
units.text: The militia of the twelve villages of Poljica, the peasant commune in the hills behind Split. Few, and hard to break on their own ground: they close a pass behind an enemy who has marched through it.

units.name: Argosy
units.text: The legendary Ragusan argosy: a massive, four-masted merchant vessel armed with cannon and crewed by 140 men. Slower than a warship but tougher and more capacious, the argosy needs no escort. It IS the escort.

units.name: Uskok Bracera
units.text: A swift, shallow-draft galley with eight oars and a crew of thirty. The bracera can navigate the narrow creeks and inlets where heavier vessels dare not follow, covering a hundred sea miles in a single night.

units.name: Pulaka
units.text: A three-masted Ragusan trader of the eighteenth century. Roomy and sailed by a small crew, it carries few guns and is no match for a frigate in a chase.

buildings.name: Fondaco
buildings.text: A Dalmatian trade warehouse and merchant exchange where goods are stored, contracts negotiated, and commercial disputes settled under the authority of the commune.

buildings.name: Hospital of Mercy
buildings.text: A foundling hospital on the model of the one Ragusa opened in 1432. Children left at its door are nursed and raised at the commune's cost, and the town's salaried physicians see the poor there.

buildings.name: General School
buildings.text: A general school on the model of the one the Dominicans keep at Zadar, where philosophy and theology are read.

buildings.name: Brotherhood Hall
buildings.text: The hall of a citizens' brotherhood, where merchants shut out of the noble councils meet, lend to one another and take shares in ships.

buildings.name: Solana
buildings.text: Salt pans kept by the commune itself. Sea water is let onto the clay flats in spring and the salt is raked in high summer. They raise the salt the shore itself gives.

where.text: The location's raw material is Salt

buildings.name: Friars' Pharmacy
buildings.text: A friary pharmacy open to the townspeople, as that of the Friars Minor of Ragusa has been since 1317. The friars compound salves and cordials for the sick of the town, and fewer of them die of a fever.

where.text: Medicaments is produced in the location's market

buildings.name: Cloth Works of Pile
buildings.text: Looms and a dye house on the model of those outside the Pile gate of Ragusa, where wool is woven, dyed and finished for sale abroad.

where.text: Wool is produced in the location's market

buildings.name: Lanterna
buildings.text: A stone light tower on a cape or a harbor mole. Ships find the harbor mouth by night, and the coast is watched from its gallery.

buildings.name: Ragusan Consulate
buildings.text: A permanent Dalmatian diplomatic and commercial office in the Ragusan tradition, where consuls manage trade agreements, gather intelligence, and represent the republic's interests with the skill of centuries of diplomatic practice.

buildings.name: Mariners' Confraternity
buildings.text: The hall and slipways of a sworn brotherhood of seamen under Saint Nicholas, of the kind the mariners of Kotor kept under their statute of 1463. The brotherhood trains crews, cares for the widows of the drowned, musters its members with their ships when the League calls the fleet, and keeps hulls ready on its own slips.

list.name: Consilium Minus
list.text: The Minor Council of Ragusa: eleven patricians who sat with the Rector as the daily government of the Republic, received envoys, heard petitions and prepared every matter that went before the larger councils. The Rector himself was chosen for a single month, lived in the palace for that month and left it only on public business, so that the office could never become a lordship. After the earthquake of 1667 the council was cut to seven. The arrangement kept government in the hands of the patrician houses at the cost of any executive power independent of them.

list.name: Grain Office
list.text: The stony coast grows wine and oil and almost no bread. Each commune therefore kept a grain office: sworn officers who bought wheat in Apulia, Sicily and the Levant with public money, shipped it home in the commune's name, stored it in the public granary and sold it to the bakers at a set price. Zadar and Split kept theirs in the fontik on the square; Ragusa cut the fifteen dry silos of the Rupe into the rock of the city, finished in 1590. A full granary kept the price of bread steady and the poor fed through siege and plague year alike, and the standing orders of its buyers kept the commune's ships and factors busy in every grain port. An empty one meant dear bread and a hungry city, where sickness spreads fastest.

list.name: Statuta Communium
list.text: The codified communal statutes of the Dalmatian cities include Korčula's law (preserved redaction 1265, traditionally dated 1214), the Vinodol Code passed 6 January 1288 in Glagolitic script (the second-oldest Slavic law after Russkaya Pravda), Zadar (1305), Split (1312), and Trogir (1322). These limited comital authority over the communes and codified self-government under elected Knez and councillors. Their refusal of judicial torture and ordeals set a Latinate-Slavic legal tradition without parallel in the Eastern Adriatic.

list.name: Stradioti Frontier Levy
list.text: From around 1475 the Venetian Dalmatian holdings of Trau, Sibenico, Castelnuovo, and Zara raised stradioti (Balkan light horse armed with spear, long saber, mace, and dagger) to hold the Ottoman frontier. They fought in the Byzantine-Slavic-Albanian tradition of hit-and-run raids, ambushes, and feigned retreats unfamiliar to western armies, and pioneered the light-cavalry doctrine that European powers spent two centuries imitating. The frontier landlords who raised them displaced the older urban militias of the coast.

list.name: Tributary Diplomacy
list.text: The strategy by which the Republic of Ragusa preserved its libertas from 1358 to 1808. The 1458 treaty with Mehmed II made the Republic a tributary of the Sultan, delivering 12,500 ducats every November to Constantinople in exchange for safe passage and tax-exempt trade across Ottoman lands, while Ragusa simultaneously remained a papal protégé. By 1800 the Republic operated consulates in more than eighty ports worldwide: the densest diplomatic apparatus per capita in early-modern Europe.
